templates.name: Hypothetical finding supports or weakens a single claim (causal, comparison, existence, generalization, prediction)
Hypothetical finding discriminates between competing explanations (support or weaken)
Quotation from a literary work illustrates a claim (single trait, two-part, contrast)
Quotation from a person (participant, respondent, historian, critic, article) supports or challenges a claim
Data description: quantified claim (for each, all except one)
Data completion: passage criterion or presence/absence combined with the display
Data completion: pairwise comparison (one or two comparisons)
Data description: trend or change over time supports a conclusion
Data completion: lookup (one cell or bar, reverse lookup, filter)
Data completion: extreme or rank (max/min, possibly after a filter)

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a proposed mechanism (rhyme read as truth; the key shows the effect fades once people attend to form)
items.passage: Proverbs that have survived for centuries frequently rhyme, prompting researchers to ask whether poetic form influences how credible such sayings seem. Matthew S. McGlone and a colleague asked participants to evaluate how accurately unfamiliar aphorisms describe human behavior, presenting each either in its original rhyming form, such as “What sobriety conceals, alcohol reveals,” or in a semantically equivalent version that did not rhyme, such as “What sobriety conceals, alcohol unmasks.” Participants judged the rhyming versions more accurate. The researchers propose that rhyme makes a statement easier to process and that people, unaware of where this ease originates, interpret it as evidence that the statement is true.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the explanation that McGlone and his colleague propose?
options: Participants rated the rhyming versions as more accurate than the altered versions whether the aphorisms concerned friendship, work, or money.
The rhyming versions lost most of their advantage when participants were first cautioned to judge each aphorism’s meaning separately from its poetic qualities.
Participants who rated the rhyming versions as more accurate explained, when asked, that a saying that rhymes has usually been tested and refined by many generations.
Participants who gave high accuracy ratings to the rhyming versions also tended to give high accuracy ratings to the altered versions that did not rhyme.
items.explanation: The researchers propose that people, “unaware of where this ease originates, interpret it as evidence that the statement is true.” If that is so, the effect should shrink once people are made to notice that some of a statement’s appeal comes from its sound rather than its sense. Choice B reports exactly that: when participants were cautioned to judge meaning separately from poetic qualities, the rhyming versions lost most of their advantage, so the advantage depended on ease that people had not been attributing to rhyme.

A.recipe: TRAP: consistent with any explanation (the effect generalizes across topics)
A.why_wrong: It shows only that rhyming versions were rated more accurate on every topic, which any account of the effect predicts; it says nothing about whether ease of processing, unnoticed, is the cause.

C.recipe: OPP: deliberate, conscious reasoning about rhyme
C.why_wrong: Participants who knowingly treat rhyme as a mark of tested wisdom are aware of why the rhyming versions persuade them, which runs against the proposal that people do not realize where their impression comes from.

D.recipe: TRAP: a correlation that cannot decide the claim
D.why_wrong: A tendency for some participants to rate all aphorisms highly is a difference between people, not between rhyming and nonrhyming forms, so it does not bear on why rhyme raises judged accuracy.

sources.what: McGlone, Tofighbakhsh 2000, Psychological Science 11(5): 424-428, Birds of a feather flock conjointly (?): rhyme as reason in aphorisms: unfamiliar rhyming aphorisms (What sobriety conceals, alcohol reveals) judged more accurate than nonrhyming versions (alcohol unmasks); the advantage was attenuated when people were cautioned to distinguish poetic qualities from semantic content; rhyme affords processing fluency misattributed to truth

items.notes: Band 7. Psychology. The key supplies the missing step (a misattribution should fade once the source of the ease is pointed out) and is the study's own reported result, worded as a hypothetical. C is the conscious-reasoning reading the proposal rules out; A and D look like evidence but cannot decide the mechanism. No option restates the passage's wording about ease. Co-author named only as a colleague (first name not confirmed). Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: key supplies an unstated premise (a misattribution is undone when its source is noticed)
two TRAP distractors (consistent with any account; a between-person correlation)
OPP is the aware, deliberate route the claim excludes
stem names the claimant, 15 words

band7.why: Passage 106 words, stem 16 words naming the claimants; the key supplies the unstated step (a misattribution fades once the source of the ease is pointed out); A and D are TRAPs that look like tests but cannot decide the mechanism, C is the aware route the claim excludes. No option restates the passage's wording.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a position in a dispute (the key supplies the cost structure that justifies a uniform price)
items.passage: Until 1840, the charge for sending a letter within Britain depended on the distance it traveled and on the number of sheets it contained, and the charge was customarily collected from the recipient on delivery. In an 1837 pamphlet, the reformer Rowland Hill proposed replacing these charges with a single inexpensive rate, prepaid by the sender, for any letter below a specified weight, regardless of whether it was crossing a town or the entire country. Critics objected that a letter transported hundreds of miles ought to cost more than one delivered locally, but Hill maintained that the distance a letter traveled was a poor basis for setting its price.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hill’s position in his dispute with the critics?
options: Carrying a letter by mail coach from London to Edinburgh cost the Post Office many times as much as carrying a letter between two neighboring towns in the same county.
After the single rate was introduced in 1840, the number of letters sent in the United Kingdom more than doubled within a year.
Many letters in the 1830s traveled free of charge because they bore the signature of a member of Parliament or another official who was exempt from postage.
Most of the Post Office’s spending on a letter went to handling it at the start and end of its journey, not to carrying it, even between distant cities.
items.explanation: Hill “maintained that the distance a letter traveled was a poor basis for setting its price,” while the critics assumed that a letter carried far costs the Post Office more than one delivered locally. Hill’s position holds only if the cost of a letter does not depend much on how far it goes. Choice D supplies that fact: if most of the expense lay in handling letters at either end and little in carrying them, a long journey costs the Post Office about as much as a short one, so distance is a poor guide to what a letter should cost.

A.recipe: OPP: the critics’ premise (cost rises with distance)
A.why_wrong: If carrying letters far cost many times more than carrying them nearby, distance would be a major source of expense, which supports the critics rather than Hill.

B.recipe: TRAP: an outcome that cannot decide the dispute
B.why_wrong: A rise in letters after the reform shows that cheaper postage drew more mail, but a lower rate that still varied with distance could have done the same; it says nothing about whether distance should set the price.

C.recipe: OFF: a true feature of the old system unrelated to distance
C.why_wrong: Free franked mail concerns who paid nothing at all, not whether the cost of a letter depends on how far it travels.

sources.what: Rowland Hill: his 1837 pamphlet Post Office Reform: its Importance and Practicability called for low and uniform rates according to weight rather than distance; his study (with Charles Babbage's findings) reported that most of the costs in the postal system were not for transport but for laborious handling procedures at the origins and destinations, and that costs could be reduced if postage were prepaid by the sender; previously postage depended on distance and number of sheets

items.notes: Band 7. History/economics. The key brings in the cost structure the passage never states (review removed the passage's pointer to where expenses originated) (handling, not carriage, as the main expense), the same move as CB's travel-cost key. B and C are true historical facts (Uniform Penny Post article: letters more than doubled in 1840; franking by MPs) that do not bear on the distance question. A is the critics' premise. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: key supplies the missing premise (a cost structure)
TRAP: a true later outcome consistent with both sides
OPP: the rival's premise
stem names whose position and the dispute, 15 words

fixes: passage: replaced 'distance-based pricing made little sense given where the Post Office’s expenses actually originated' (it named the key's premise) with 'the distance a letter traveled was a poor basis for setting its price', so the key supplies an unstated cost structure; explanation requoted

band7.why: After the fix the passage no longer names the premise: the key brings in the cost structure (handling, not carriage) that the critics' objection silently assumes away, as in CB 64cd7321 and 3.28. B is a true later outcome that cannot decide the dispute (TRAP), A the critics' premise (OPP), C off-target.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a proposed cause of a pattern (uphill seed dispersal by bears following the fruiting season)
items.passage: Plants threatened by a warming climate can persist by colonizing cooler terrain at higher elevations, but only if their seeds are transported there. Because the ratio of oxygen isotopes in a cherry pit reflects the elevation at which its parent tree grew, Shoji Naoe and colleagues could compare where seeds of the wild cherry Prunus jamasakura were deposited in the droppings of Asiatic black bears in Japan with where those seeds originated: most had been carried uphill, some by several hundred meters. The researchers attribute this asymmetry to the bears’ habit of tracking the ripening of cherries as the fruiting season progresses.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Naoe and colleagues’ explanation of the pattern?
options: Cherry trees growing high on the slopes ripened their fruit several weeks later in the season than cherry trees growing lower down did.
Seeds that bears swallowed late in the fruiting season were more often deposited below the trees that produced them than seeds swallowed early in the season were.
Japanese martens, which also eat wild cherries in the study area, carried the seeds they swallowed shorter distances uphill than the bears did.
Cherry seeds recovered from the bears’ droppings sprouted about as often as seeds that the researchers had picked directly from the trees.
items.explanation: The researchers attribute the uphill dispersal to bears’ “habit of tracking the ripening of cherries as the fruiting season progresses.” That explanation works only if ripening itself moves uphill over the season. Choice A supplies that premise: if fruit ripens weeks later on upper slopes, a bear that follows the ripening fruit moves higher as the season goes on, so seeds it swallowed lower down are deposited above the trees that produced them.

B.why_wrong: If bears following the season carried late seeds downhill, their movements over the season would not produce the uphill pattern, which weakens the explanation.

C.recipe: TRAP: a comparison of dispersers that cannot decide the cause
C.why_wrong: That martens carried seeds less far uphill says nothing about why bears carry them uphill; it would be equally true whatever the cause of the bears’ pattern.

D.recipe: OFF: seed survival rather than direction of dispersal
D.why_wrong: Whether swallowed seeds still sprout concerns the value of bears as dispersers, not why the seeds they carry end up higher.

sources.what: Naoe, Tayasu, Sakai, Masaki, Kobayashi, Nakajima, Sato, Yamazaki, Kiyokawa, Koike 2016, Current Biology 26(8): R315-316: stable oxygen isotope shows black bears disperse wild cherry seeds several hundred meters vertically, biased toward mountain tops; mountain climbing by bears following spring-to-summer plant phenology is the likely cause

items.notes: Band 6 (plan). Life science. The key needs two linked steps (fruit ripens later higher up; bears track it). B is the reversed seasonal direction; C and D engage the same animals and seeds but not the cause. The study's cherry is Prunus jamasakura (the paper's 'wild cherry'); martens are a plausible co-disperser offered only as a hypothetical finding. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.

fixes: key A cut to the ripening-lag premise alone ('...and the bears fed progressively higher as the season went on' restated the explanation); explanation rewritten

band7.why: Planned band 6. With the key cut to the ripening lag alone, the student must link later ripening upslope to bears that follow ripe fruit carrying seeds uphill (two steps). C (martens) is a comparison that cannot decide the cause; B and D are easier.

items.subtype: Finding that discriminates rival explanations (two single-route migration hypotheses against arrival from more than one direction)
items.passage: According to the long-dominant Out of Taiwan hypothesis, the first farming communities of Island Southeast Asia descended from migrants who moved south from Taiwan into the Philippines and then onward to Borneo and Indonesia, bringing pottery with them; a rival proposal, the Western Route Migration hypothesis, holds that the earliest farmers instead entered the islands from mainland Southeast Asia to the west. Using radiocarbon dates from 20 archaeological sites, Ethan E. Cochrane, Timothy M. Rieth, and Dennis Filimoehala estimated when pottery first appeared at each, treating its appearance as a marker of the newcomers’ arrival. They concluded that the evidence fits neither hypothesis alone and that settlement proceeded in more than one direction.
items.stem: Which finding from the study, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: The earliest pottery at sites in the northern Philippines is several centuries older than the earliest pottery at sites in Borneo and eastern Indonesia.
At most of the sites, the oldest layers containing pottery also contain the remains of plants or animals that people had domesticated.
Pottery first appeared in western Borneo at about the same time as in the northern Philippines, the part of the islands nearest Taiwan.
Pottery from sites in the Philippines was more often decorated with red pigment than pottery from sites in Borneo was.
items.explanation: Under the Out of Taiwan hypothesis, pottery should appear first in the north, near Taiwan, and later farther south; under the Western Route hypothesis, it should appear first in the west, nearest the mainland. Choice C reports that pottery appeared at about the same time in western Borneo and in the northern Philippines. Neither single route predicts that pattern, but arrivals from more than one direction do, so the finding supports the conclusion that settlement “proceeded in more than one direction.”

A.recipe: OPP: the Out of Taiwan prediction
A.why_wrong: Pottery that is oldest in the north and younger to the south is the pattern a single southward movement from Taiwan predicts, so it would support that hypothesis rather than the researchers’ conclusion.

B.why_wrong: Every hypothesis in the passage holds that the newcomers were farmers who brought pottery, so finding pottery with domesticated remains cannot tell the routes apart.

D.recipe: OFF: an irrelevant property of the same pottery
D.why_wrong: Differences in decoration between regions say nothing about when pottery arrived in each, which is what bears on the direction of settlement.

sources.what: Cochrane, Rieth, Filimoehala 2021, PLoS ONE 16(6): e0251407: Out of Taiwan (south from Taiwan) vs Western Route Migration (from Mainland Southeast Asia in the west) hypotheses; Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates from 20 sites; results indicate multi-directional Neolithic dispersal, with the earliest pottery contemporaneously deposited in western Borneo and the northern Philippines

items.notes: Band 6 (plan). Archaeology. The key must be read against both rival predictions (north first, or west first); only simultaneity fits the multi-directional conclusion. A is the Out of Taiwan prediction (OPP), B is consistent with all three views (TRAP), D is an irrelevant property of the same objects. The red-slip decoration detail is a hypothetical finding, not from the paper. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

band7.why: Planned band 6. The key must be read against both rival predictions (north first, or west first); only simultaneity in western Borneo and the northern Philippines fits more than one direction. A is the Out of Taiwan prediction, B fits every view; D is an easy OFF.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates an indirect claim (resignation that betrays reluctance; drama)
items.passage: Chains is a 1909 play by Elizabeth Baker. Charley Wilson, a London clerk, abandons a secret plan to emigrate to Australia upon learning that his wife is expecting a child. Afterward, Charley intimates that he has relinquished the plan reluctantly while attempting to persuade himself that remaining in London is preferable, saying, ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Chains most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Get over it? I’m not going to get over anything. I’ve been a coward, see?—and now I’m going to cut and run.”
“No, the thing was meant to be! I was mad. After all, a man can’t do just what he likes! It’s better as it is.”
“Why not? Why not? If I put it off, I’ll never go. It wants a bit of doing, and if you don’t do these things at the time, well, you give in.”
“I’ve got a short neck. I suppose you shouldn’t be a clerk, if you’ve got a short neck. It doesn’t fit the collars.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Charley gives up the plan reluctantly, and he tries to convince himself that staying is best. In choice B, “a man can’t do just what he likes!” implies that he would still like to go, which shows the reluctance, while “the thing was meant to be!” and “It’s better as it is” are the reassurances he offers himself for staying.

A.recipe: OPP: the same speaker resolved to leave
A.why_wrong: Here Charley is determined to go (“I’m going to cut and run”); he has not given up the plan at all.

C.recipe: LURE: mentions giving in, but as something he refuses to do
C.why_wrong: Charley fears that delay would make him “give in,” but he says this to push himself to leave now, not to accept staying.

D.recipe: HALF: the same speaker after giving up, chafing without self-persuasion
D.why_wrong: Charley’s joke that a man with a short neck “shouldn’t be a clerk” hints that he still chafes at the life he is returning to, but it offers no reassurance that staying is better; if anything, it suggests the opposite.

sources.what: Elizabeth Baker, Chains: A Play, in Four Acts (London: Sidgwick & Jackson, 1911; first performed 1909); Charley Wilson's lines from several scenes; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (double hyphens rendered as closed em dashes)

items.notes: Band 7. Drama, first staged 1909 (published 1911). All four options are Charley in neighboring states: resolve (A), urgency against giving in (C), chafing at clerk life after giving up, with no self-persuasion (D, the collar lines just before he leaves for the office), and reluctant self-persuasion after giving up (B). B begins at a sentence boundary within his final-act speech to his sister-in-law Maggie. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: indirect claim verb (intimates) with a two-part stance
distractors are the same speaker in nearby states (resolve, urgency) and after giving up (chafing, no self-persuasion)
keyword lure (give in)

fixes: D replaced: 'It’s that I’m just sick of the office...' (pre-abandonment, ruled out by the same fact as A and C) with Charley’s collar lines from the final scene (exact Gutenberg text), a post-abandonment HALF that shows reluctance but no self-persuasion, as in the Richard II band-7 model
review.notes: all four options exact substrings of Gutenberg 46240; all Charley's.

band7.why: Indirect claim verb (intimates) with two parts; after the fix the options are Charley resolved to go (A), urging himself not to give in (C), and, after giving up, chafing at clerk life without any self-persuasion (D), so no single fact kills all three, as in the Richard II band-7 model.

items.subtype: Quotation from an art historian supports a claim made inside a rebuttal (paintings read as records of country, not form alone)
items.passage: In the early 1980s, Rover Thomas, a Wangkajunga and Kukatja artist who had worked for decades as a stockman in the Kimberley region of Western Australia, began painting with natural ochres on canvas. His spare compositions—broad fields of earth color interrupted by a few contours, some outlined in dots—are frequently likened to the canvases of Western abstract painters. Such comparisons are understandable, a student argues, but they become misleading if they encourage viewers to treat the paintings as arrangements of shape and color alone, since each of Thomas’s works records a particular stretch of country and the events, recent or ancestral, that occurred there.
items.stem: Which quotation from an art historian would most directly support the student’s argument?
options: “What a European eye reads as a floating black form is, for Thomas, an actual hill or waterhole, and a band of dots may trace a road or a creek; a single canvas can carry the story of what happened at that place, as Thomas had heard it told or had lived it.”

“The force of Thomas’s paintings lies in their economy: a handful of shapes in a narrow range of ochres, placed so that the eye registers mass, edge, and interval before anything else. It is as a master of these formal relationships that he belongs beside the great abstract painters of the twentieth century.”

“The resemblance between Thomas’s canvases and Western abstraction is best explained by shared means rather than shared aims: like many abstract painters, he worked in flat, matte fields of color and favored large formats in which a few forms could dominate the picture.”

“Thomas’s ochres, dug from the earth of the East Kimberley, give his canvases a dry, granular surface quite unlike the smooth finish of the oil and acrylic paints used by most of the abstract painters with whom he is so often compared.”
items.explanation: The student argues that comparisons with abstract painting mislead if they lead viewers to see only shape and color, “since each of Thomas’s works records a particular stretch of country and the events, recent or ancestral, that occurred there.” Choice A supports exactly that point: forms that look abstract to a European viewer stand for a specific hill, waterhole, road, or creek, and a canvas carries the story of what happened at that place.

B.recipe: OPP: sides with the purely formal reading the student rejects
B.why_wrong: It locates the paintings’ value in shape, edge, and interval and ranks Thomas among abstract painters on those grounds, the view the student says is misleading.

C.recipe: TRAP: explains the resemblance without the claim
C.why_wrong: It accounts for why the paintings look like abstractions, by shared methods, but it never says what the paintings record, so it does not show that they depict particular places and events.

D.recipe: HALF: ties the materials to the region, not the subject
D.why_wrong: It connects Thomas’s ochres to the East Kimberley and contrasts his surfaces with abstract painters’, but where the pigment came from does not show that each painting records a particular place and what happened there.

sources.what: Rover Thomas Joolama (1926-1998), Wangkajunga and Kukatja artist; stockman in the Kimberley, later at Turkey Creek (Warmun); painted Krill Krill ceremony boards from 1977; began painting ochre on canvas in the early 1980s (East Kimberley School); paintings of massacre sites (Bedford Downs Massacre) described by an NGV curator as describing actual events remembered in oral history while also being planar constructions of colour and form; often compared to Rothko; first Aboriginal artist at the Venice Biennale (1990)

items.notes: Band 7. Arts. The claim sits inside the student's rebuttal of the formalist comparison (as in CB's Fred Stevens item). Quotations are from an unnamed art historian and stay general (hills, waterholes, roads, events) rather than describing a particular canvas. B argues the rejected view; C reconciles the resemblance without the claim; D is a true-sounding link to the land through materials only. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: claim inside a rebuttal
quotations of about 45 to 55 words that argue
OPP (the rejected view), TRAP (a reconciliation that misses the claim), HALF

fixes: key A: 'a particular hill or waterhole' to 'an actual hill or waterhole' (echoed 'a particular stretch of country')

band7.why: Claim sits inside the student's rebuttal; quotations of about 45 to 55 words that argue; B sides with the rejected formal reading (OPP), C reconciles the resemblance without the claim (TRAP), D links the paintings to the land through materials only (HALF). Key's echo of 'particular' removed.

items.subtype: Data completion (treatments against an unprimed baseline of 1.00; one treatment that raises one measure and lowers the other)
items.passage: Soaking seeds in a solution before sowing, a technique known as priming, can help seedlings tolerate saline soil. Xiaofei Chen and colleagues primed seeds of sorghum, a cereal cultivated widely in dry regions, in several different solutions, grew them in salty water, and compared the resulting seedlings with seedlings from unprimed seeds grown under identical conditions, expressing every result relative to the unprimed seedlings’ value of 1.00. Their results show that a single priming treatment can affect growth below and above the ground in opposite directions: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: seedlings from seeds primed with potassium chloride had roots nearly 1.5 times as long as those of unprimed seedlings, yet their shoots weighed less.
seedlings from seeds primed with calcium chloride had both longer roots and heavier shoots than seedlings from unprimed seeds did.
seedlings from seeds primed with water had roots about 1.5 times as long as those of unprimed seedlings, yet their shoots weighed slightly less.
seedlings from seeds primed with polyethylene glycol had roots only about half as long as those of unprimed seedlings, yet their shoots weighed more.

table.title: Root Length and Shoot Dry Weight of Seedlings from Primed Sorghum Seeds under Salt Stress, Relative to Unprimed Seeds
table.note: A value of 1.00 equals the result for unprimed seeds under the same salt stress.

items.explanation: The statement needs a treatment that moved growth below and above the ground in opposite directions relative to the unprimed value of 1.00. Seedlings from seeds primed with water had a relative root length of 1.55, so their roots were about one and a half times as long, but a relative shoot dry weight of 0.90, below that of unprimed seedlings. Choice C therefore completes the statement.

A.recipe: INACC: a value above 1.00 read as below
A.why_wrong: Seedlings from seeds primed with potassium chloride had a relative shoot dry weight of 1.07, so their shoots weighed slightly more than those of unprimed seedlings, not less.

B.recipe: IRREL/CONTRA: accurate, but both measures move the same way
B.why_wrong: Calcium chloride did raise both values (2.20 and 1.47), but an improvement in both measures is not an effect in opposite directions.

D.recipe: WDIR: the 1.00 baseline applied the wrong way
D.why_wrong: A relative root length of 1.74 means roots about 1.7 times as long as those of unprimed seedlings, not about half as long.

sources.what: Chen, Zhang, Xing, Jiang, Li, Xu et al. 2021, PLoS ONE 16(1): e0245505, The efficacy of different seed priming agents for promoting sorghum germination under salt stress (Shenyang Agricultural University): priming with water, NaCl, KCl, CaCl2 and PEG under 150 mM NaCl; Table 2 relative values (to unprimed seeds under salt): relative root length HP 1.55, 50KCl 1.46, 50CaCl2 2.20, 10%PEG 1.74; relative shoot dry weight HP 0.90, 50KCl 1.07, 50CaCl2 1.47, 10%PEG 1.16; text: all traits higher with water priming except shoot dry weight

items.notes: Band 6 (plan). Agricultural science. Four of the paper's treatments shown; germination columns left out so the item does not echo CB 2.5 (seed germination after treatment). The display must be read through the 1.00 baseline the passage and note define; D misapplies it, A reads 1.07 as a decrease, B is accurate but the wrong pattern. Only water priming moves the two measures in opposite directions. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

review.notes: values match Table 2 of the PLoS ONE paper (PMC7815140): RRL 1.55/1.46/2.20/1.74, RSDW 0.90/1.07/1.47/1.16.

band7.why: Planned band 6. The 1.00 baseline from the passage and note must be applied to two columns of four rows; A mirrors the key with one misread value (1.07 as less), D misapplies the baseline, B is accurate but the wrong pattern. A careful scan settles it, so not band 7.

items.subtype: Data description (a change in every region plus a majority in all regions but one)
items.passage: Noncommunicable diseases, such as heart disease, stroke, cancer, and diabetes, are not transmitted from person to person, unlike infections such as malaria or tuberculosis. As countries reduce deaths from infectious diseases and their populations age, noncommunicable diseases typically account for a growing proportion of deaths, a pattern widely known as the epidemiological transition. Examining World Health Organization estimates, a student asserts that between 2000 and 2019 the share of deaths caused by noncommunicable diseases increased in each of five world regions and that by 2019 such diseases accounted for a majority of deaths in all of those regions but one.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s assertion?
options: The smallest change in any region between 2000 and 2019 was North America’s rise of 0.4 percentage points, and Sub-Saharan Africa’s 35.8% was the only share below 50% in 2019.
South Asia’s share rose from 38.9% to 68.2% between 2000 and 2019, the largest increase of any region, so that by 2019 most deaths there were caused by noncommunicable diseases.
In both 2000 and 2019, North America had the largest share of any region and Sub-Saharan Africa had the smallest, though Sub-Saharan Africa’s share rose by more than 15 percentage points.
Each region’s share was higher in 2019 than in 2000, and in 2000 the share was below 50% only in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa.

table.title: Share of Deaths Caused by Noncommunicable Diseases in Five Regions, 2000 and 2019 (%)

items.explanation: The student makes two assertions: the share rose “in each of five world regions,” and by 2019 it was a majority “in all of those regions but one.” Choice A supports both. If the smallest change in any region, North America’s move from 87.9% to 88.3%, was a rise of 0.4 percentage points, then every region’s share rose; and if Sub-Saharan Africa’s 35.8% was the only 2019 share below 50%, the other four regions all had majorities.

B.why_wrong: The figures for South Asia are accurate, but one region cannot show that the share rose in each of the five or that only one region lacked a majority.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate ranking of the extremes
C.why_wrong: Which regions had the largest and smallest shares, and one region’s increase, say nothing about whether every region’s share rose or how many regions passed 50%.

D.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but the second part read from the wrong year
D.why_wrong: Both clauses are accurate, but the second describes 2000, when two regions were below 50%; it says nothing about 2019, when only Sub-Saharan Africa was, so it does not support the student’s claim about 2019.

sources.what: World Bank indicator SH.DTH.NCOM.ZS, Cause of death, by non-communicable diseases (% of total), source WHO Global Health Estimates; 2000 and 2019 values for East Asia & Pacific 75.3/85.5, Latin America & Caribbean 66.8/74.9, North America 87.9/88.3, South Asia 38.9/68.2, Sub-Saharan Africa 20.6/35.8

items.notes: Band 7. Public health/geography. Two quantified parts (a rise in every region; a majority in all but one). North America's rise of 0.4 points makes the first check a real one. B and C are accurate but insufficient; D is accurate but reads the second part from 2000 (review rewrite); the key is indirect, as CB 3.24. Values checked against the World Bank API on 2026-10-27; 2019 chosen to avoid COVID-19 years. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: every-region-plus-majority quantifier (the trap of CB 3.24)
two accurate-but-insufficient distractors
an accurate distractor that reads the second part from the wrong year

fixes: key A rewritten indirectly (the smallest change was a rise; the only 2019 share below 50%), as CB 3.24, instead of restating the assertion; D rewritten from a mirror of the key with one false clause to an accurate first clause plus a 2000 second clause (wrong year); explanation and D why_wrong rewritten

band7.why: Every-region-plus-majority quantifier, the band-7 trap named in the doc (CB 3.24). After the fix the key is indirect (the smallest change was a rise, so all rose), North America's 0.4-point rise makes the first check real, D is accurate but reads the second part from 2000, B is one region, C accurate extremes.

items.subtype: Data completion (passage thresholds and a per-person proxy applied to two years; conclusion about two countries)
items.passage: Hydrologist Malin Falkenmark proposed assessing a country’s water situation by dividing its renewable freshwater resources by its population: below 1,700 cubic meters per person per year, a country is considered to experience water stress, and below 1,000, water scarcity. Because the quantity of renewable water generated within a country changes little from decade to decade, the figure per person declines mainly as the population grows. Examining World Bank estimates for five African countries, a student observes that two countries whose supplies per person fell by comparable amounts between 2000 and 2020 nonetheless ended the period in different categories: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Burkina Faso’s and Kenya’s supplies each fell by about 470 cubic meters per person, yet only Burkina Faso had moved from water stress into water scarcity by 2020, while Kenya had been experiencing scarcity since 2000.
Ethiopia’s supply fell by about 780 cubic meters per person and Uganda’s by about 750, yet by 2020 only Uganda’s supply had fallen below the threshold for water scarcity.
Senegal’s and Ethiopia’s supplies fell by similar amounts, but by 2020 Senegal had entered water scarcity while Ethiopia was experiencing only water stress.
Uganda’s and Ethiopia’s total renewable freshwater resources each shrank by more than 40 percent, leaving Uganda in water scarcity and Ethiopia under water stress by 2020.

table.title: Renewable Freshwater Generated within Each Country (cubic meters per person per year)

items.explanation: The student needs two countries whose figures fell by nearly the same amount but that ended in different categories. Ethiopia fell from 1,810 to 1,026 cubic meters per person (about 780) and Uganda from 1,625 to 877 (about 750). By 2020 Ethiopia, at 1,026, was below the 1,700 threshold for water stress but above the 1,000 threshold for water scarcity, while Uganda, at 877, was below 1,000. Choice B completes the statement.

A.recipe: INACC: a false similarity (and no difference in final category)
A.why_wrong: Burkina Faso’s figure fell by about 470 cubic meters per person but Kenya’s by only about 280, and both countries were in water scarcity by 2020, so they did not end in different categories.

C.why_wrong: Senegal’s 2020 figure of 1,537 is above 1,000, so by the passage’s thresholds it was in water stress, not scarcity; its decline (about 1,050) was also much larger than Ethiopia’s.

D.recipe: OUTS: a claim about totals the per-person data cannot show
D.why_wrong: The table shows water per person, and the passage says the total a country generates changes little; the per-person declines reflect population growth, not shrinking total resources.

sources.what: World Bank indicator ER.H2O.INTR.PC, Renewable internal freshwater resources per capita (cubic meters), 2000 and 2020: Burkina Faso 1,048/582, Ethiopia 1,810/1,026, Kenya 676/396, Senegal 2,588/1,537, Uganda 1,625/877 (values rounded; checked against the API on 2026-10-27)
Falkenmark Water Stress Indicator (Malin Falkenmark): water stress below 1,700 cubic meters per person per year, water scarcity below 1,000

items.notes: Band 7. Geography/environment. The passage states two thresholds and the proxy relation (per-person figures fall with population); the key needs four reads, two subtractions, a similarity judgment, and two threshold checks. D is the band-7 proxy trap: accurate per-person percentages (about 46 and 43) recast as totals. Only Ethiopia and Uganda form a pair with similar declines and different 2020 categories. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found. Lead 2026-10-27: 'nearly identical' changed to 'comparable' (784 vs 748 per safety solve).
band7_moves: passage criterion and proxy applied to the display
conclusion about countries, not about cells
OUTS trap through the proxy (totals vs per person)
compound options of 25 to 35 words
five or more operations

band7.why: Passage states two thresholds and the per-person proxy; the key needs four reads, two subtractions, a similarity judgment and two threshold checks; D is the OUTS trap through the proxy (totals vs per person), A and C are compounds with false clauses; options 25 to 35 words.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (a cost accepted and a relief expected; drama)
items.passage: The Voysey Inheritance is a 1905 play by Harley Granville-Barker. Edward Voysey, a young solicitor, has discovered that his father, the head of the family firm, misappropriated clients’ investments for years. Edward suggests that publicly exposing the fraud will be personally costly but will also liberate him from an oppressive burden of shame: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Voysey Inheritance most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “The Law’s no respecter of persons . . that’s its boast. Old Booth with more than he wants will keep enough. My old nurse, with just enough, may starve.”
“I can’t let myself be glad and live. There’s the future to think of. And I’m so afraid of that. I must pretend I don’t care . . even to myself . . even to you.”
“But it’ll be a relief to clear out this nest of lies, even though one suffers one’s self. I’ve been ashamed to walk into that office, Alice . . I’ll hold my head high in prison though.”
“Look, all I’ve been able to do in this business . . at the cost of my whole life perhaps . . has been to sit senselessly by my father’s side and prevent things going from bad to worse.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: exposing the fraud will be personally costly for Edward, and it will liberate him from shame. In choice C he expects to suffer, even to go to “prison,” yet calls clearing out “this nest of lies” “a relief” and says that although he has “been ashamed to walk into that office,” he will “hold [his] head high” afterward. Only this quotation contains both the cost and the release from shame.

A.recipe: OFF: harm to the clients, not to Edward
A.why_wrong: Edward describes how the law will treat the firm’s clients unequally, but he says nothing about what exposure will cost him or about his shame.

B.recipe: HALF: fear of the future without relief
B.why_wrong: Edward voices fear of what lies ahead but no sense that anything will free him from shame.

D.recipe: LURE: a cost to Edward, but of the past cover-up
D.why_wrong: The cost Edward names is the life he has spent keeping things from getting worse at his father’s side, not the price of exposing the fraud, and he expresses no relief.

sources.what: Harley Granville-Barker, The Voysey Inheritance (first performed 1905; text in Three Plays by Granville-Barker, 1909); Edward Voysey's speeches, most to Alice; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text, keeping the author's two-dot pauses

items.notes: Medium. Drama. Granville-Barker marks pauses with two spaced dots; they are kept as printed. A and C come from the same speech; D carries the lure word cost. Play premiered at the Court Theatre in 1905. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

review.notes: all four options exact substrings of Gutenberg 35640.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (dreary marriage and separation from a loved world; drama)
items.passage: The New York Idea is a 1906 play by Langdon Mitchell. On the day she is to marry Philip Phillimore, a conventional and rather humorless judge, Cynthia Karslake, a divorced socialite passionately devoted to horse racing, anticipates that married life will be monotonous and that she will be painfully separated from the racing world: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The New York Idea most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Nervous! Of course I’m nervous! So would you be nervous if you’d had a runaway and smash up, and you were going to try it again.”
“I fancied Hermes would come in an easy winner. He came in nowhere. Nonpareil was ridden by Henslow—he’s a rotten bad rider. He gets nervous.”
“But the whim’s gone flat! Yes, yes, my gasoline days are over. I’m going to be garaged for good.”
“When Philip’s fallen asleep, and little boys are crying [calling out] the winners outside, and I’m crying inside, and dying inside and outside and everywhere.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: married life will be monotonous, and Cynthia will be painfully separated from the racing world. In choice D she pictures evenings after “Philip’s fallen asleep,” while boys outside call out the race “winners” and she is “crying inside”: the racing news goes on outside while she is shut in, unhappy, with a sleeping husband.

A.recipe: LURE: horse imagery for fear of remarrying
A.why_wrong: Cynthia compares a second marriage to riding again after a runaway, which shows nervousness, not an expectation that married life will be monotonous or keep her from racing.

B.why_wrong: This shows her keen interest in racing but says nothing about her marriage to Philip or about being separated from that world.

C.recipe: HALF: a settled life, cheerfully accepted
C.why_wrong: She jokes that her days of fast living are over, but she mentions neither racing nor any pain at the change.

sources.what: Langdon Mitchell, The New York Idea (first performed at the Lyric Theatre, New York, November 19, 1906), in Representative Plays by American Dramatists 1856-1911; Philip Phillimore is a judge; Cynthia's lines from several scenes; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (double hyphens as closed em dashes)

items.notes: Medium. Drama. The key begins at a sentence boundary in Cynthia's wedding-day speech about orange blossoms ("They smell of six o'clock in the evening. When Philip's fallen asleep..."). Crying the winners: newsboys calling race results; a CB-style bracketed gloss [calling out] is added, and the student still infers that the winners are race results from the passage's racing context. A and C use motoring and horse figures that lure without both parts. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.

review.notes: batch note checked: C ('garaged for good') is not defensible. In the play the whim that has 'gone flat' is the one Sir Wilfrid supposes she has for him, and 'gasoline days'/'garaged' is a cheerful motoring joke: no racing, no pain. The [calling out] gloss is CB style.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim about how objects were made (local production adapted to local materials)
items.passage: The Tumaco tradition thrived along the Pacific coast of what is now southwestern Colombia, and clay figurines from its settlements share a recognizable style. Nohora Alba Bustamante and colleagues studied figurines made between about 350 BCE and 350 CE at two Tumaco sites, Inguapí and La Cocotera. They hypothesized that despite this shared style, the figurines were not made by a single group of specialists; instead, potters at each site developed their own techniques, suited to the materials available nearby.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Bustamante and colleagues’ hypothesis?
options: The clay in each site’s figurines matches clay found near that site, and the two sites shaped and finished their figurines differently.
The figurines from both sites were made from clay taken from a single deposit and were fired at the same temperature in the same kind of pit.
The figurines from both sites depict human figures, and traces of paint survive on nearly all of them.
Pottery vessels from Inguapí were made from a different clay than pottery vessels from sites of the same period in present-day Ecuador.
items.explanation: The researchers hypothesized that “potters at each site developed their own techniques, suited to the materials available nearby.” If the clay in each site’s figurines matches clay found near that site and the two sites shaped and finished their figurines differently, then each site was using its own materials and its own methods. Choice A supports the hypothesis.

B.recipe: OPP: one shared source and process
B.why_wrong: A single clay source and identical firing would suggest one shared production, the opposite of separate local traditions.

C.why_wrong: That figurines from both sites show human figures and were painted reflects the shared style the passage already mentions; it says nothing about where or how each site made them.

D.recipe: SUBJ: other objects and other places
D.why_wrong: It compares pottery vessels from Inguapí with vessels from Ecuador, not the figurines from the two Tumaco sites the hypothesis concerns.

sources.what: Bustamante, Escobar, Martinón-Torres 2021, PLoS ONE 16(5): e0250230, Reverse engineering of ceramic anthropomorphic figurines from the Tumaco archaeological tradition in southwest Colombia: figurines from Inguapí and La Cocotera (350 BC-AD 350) show two manufacturing pathways developed locally and adapted to the natural resources available to each site (chemical and mineralogical differences in raw materials, differences in preparation, shaping, molding and modeling); all figurines painted; shared technical style

items.notes: Medium. Archaeology. One bridge: local materials and distinct methods at each site. B is the single-workshop prediction, C restates the shared style, D shifts to other objects and regions. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Data completion (two comparisons at once: above one species, below another)
items.passage: The harlequin ladybird (Harmonia axyridis), native to Asia, has been released in numerous countries to control aphids and other agricultural pests, and it now competes with native ladybirds in cornfields in Mexico. Morelia Camacho-Cervantes and colleagues placed ladybirds of four species in containers with 10 aphids each and recorded how many aphids each beetle consumed. The results suggest that the introduced species was neither the most nor the least effective predator of the four: on average, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: the harlequin ladybird ate 2.3 aphids per trial, more than Paranaemia vittigera did but fewer than Cycloneda sanguinea did.
the harlequin ladybird ate more aphids per trial than Hippodamia convergens did but fewer aphids per trial than Paranaemia vittigera did.
the harlequin ladybird ate 1.6 aphids per trial, more than Paranaemia vittigera’s 1.1 but fewer than Cycloneda sanguinea’s 2.9.
the harlequin ladybird ate about 1.6 aphids per trial, fewer than any of the three native species ate.

table.title: Average Number of Aphids Eaten per Trial by Four Ladybird Species

items.explanation: To show that the harlequin ladybird was “neither the most nor the least effective predator of the four,” the choice must place it above at least one species and below at least one. The table shows that it ate 1.6 aphids per trial, more than Paranaemia vittigera (1.1) and fewer than Cycloneda sanguinea (2.9). Choice C completes the statement.

A.why_wrong: 2.3 aphids per trial is the figure for Hippodamia convergens; the harlequin ladybird ate 1.6.

B.why_wrong: The harlequin ladybird ate fewer aphids than Hippodamia convergens (1.6 against 2.3) and more than Paranaemia vittigera (1.6 against 1.1), the reverse of what this choice says.

D.why_wrong: Paranaemia vittigera ate only 1.1 aphids per trial, fewer than the harlequin ladybird, so the harlequin ladybird was not the least effective predator.

sources.what: Camacho-Cervantes, Mendoza-Arroyo, Arellano-Sánchez, del-Val 2021, PeerJ 9: e12503, Exotic predators are not better biocontrol agents: the harlequin ladybird is not the most voracious in Mexico: 10 aphids (Aphis fabae) per container; mean aphids consumed by species: H. axyridis 1.6, H. convergens 2.3, C. sanguinea 2.9, P. vittigera 1.1 (means over all trial types)

items.notes: Medium. Life science. Two comparisons in one option; distractors are a misplaced value, a full reversal, and a false extreme. Means are pooled over trials with one or two beetles, as in the paper's species rows. The paper reports the harlequin and H. convergens difference as not significant, so no option relies on it. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

review.notes: values match the species rows of PMC8603833 (1.6, 2.3, 2.9, 1.1).

items.subtype: Data description (rapid growth after a set year and one country overtaking another by the final year)
items.passage: Lomé, the capital of Togo, has one of the few natural deep-water ports on the West African coast. It functions as a transshipment hub, where containers are transferred between large oceangoing vessels and smaller ships bound for other ports in the region. Examining World Bank data on container traffic, measured in twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), a student concludes that Togo’s traffic expanded dramatically in the late 2010s. By 2020, the student argues, it exceeded Nigeria’s, even though Nigeria’s population is more than 25 times larger than Togo’s.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student’s conclusion?
options: Togo’s container traffic was lower than both Nigeria’s and Ghana’s in 2010, 2012, and 2014.
Togo’s traffic grew from about 0.4 million TEUs in 2014 to about 1.7 million in 2020, surpassing Nigeria’s 1.5 million.
Togo’s container traffic rose between every pair of years shown, and it was greater than Ghana’s container traffic in every year from 2016 onward.
Nigeria’s container traffic peaked in 2014 at about 1.9 million TEUs and then fell to about 1.3 million TEUs in 2016.

figure.title: Container Traffic at the Ports of Three West African Countries, 2010–2020
figure.description: Three lines at 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2020; y-axis 0 to 2.0 in steps of 0.2. Togo: about 0.34, 0.29, 0.38, 0.82, 1.40, 1.73 (low and nearly flat to 2014, then a steep rise). Nigeria: about 1.16, 1.58, 1.87, 1.27, 1.56, 1.55 (a peak in 2014, a drop in 2016, then nearly level). Ghana: about 0.64, 0.88, 0.79, 0.94, 1.06, 1.32 (a gradual rise). Togo is below both other countries through 2014 and above both in 2020.

items.explanation: The student concludes that Togo’s traffic “expanded dramatically in the late 2010s” and that by 2020 “it exceeded Nigeria’s.” The graph shows Togo rising from about 0.4 million TEUs in 2014 to about 1.7 million in 2020, more than four times as much, and in 2020 Togo’s line is above Nigeria’s, which is at about 1.5 million. Choice B reports both the rapid growth and the overtaking.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but the period before the growth
A.why_wrong: Togo’s low traffic through 2014 is accurate, but it says nothing about the growth that followed or about Togo exceeding Nigeria by 2020.

C.recipe: INACC: a false steady rise and a false comparison
C.why_wrong: Togo’s traffic dipped from about 0.34 to about 0.29 million TEUs between 2010 and 2012, and in 2016 Togo (about 0.82) was still below Ghana (about 0.94).

D.why_wrong: Nigeria’s peak and decline are read correctly, but they say nothing about Togo’s growth and do not compare the two countries in 2020.

sources.what: World Bank indicator IS.SHP.GOOD.TU, Container port traffic (TEU: 20 foot equivalent units), 2010-2020: Togo 0.34, 0.29, 0.38, 0.82, 1.40, 1.73 million; Nigeria 1.16, 1.58, 1.87, 1.27, 1.56, 1.55; Ghana 0.64, 0.88, 0.79, 0.94, 1.06, 1.32 (checked against the API on 2026-10-27); 2020 populations Nigeria 214.0 million, Togo 7.8 million (SP.POP.TOTL)
Lomé: one of the few natural deep-water ports on the West African coast, a container transshipment hub (Lomé Container Terminal)

items.notes: Medium. Geography/economics. Two-part trend (growth after 2014, overtaking by 2020). A and D are accurate but address the wrong period or country; C is a false reading. The terminal's opening year is left out because it could not be confirmed from a fetched page. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.

fixes: key B and explanation: Nigeria's 2020 traffic 'about 1.6 million' to 'about 1.5 million' (World Bank 1,548,622)

items.subtype: Data completion (the weakest treatment against the untreated control at one time point)
items.passage: Ponkan, a variety of mandarin orange cultivated widely in southern China, deteriorates readily during prolonged storage. Qiang Huang and colleagues coated freshly harvested Ponkan fruit with solutions of gum arabic, a natural gum obtained from acacia trees, at several concentrations, stored the coated fruit alongside uncoated fruit at 10°C for 120 days, and periodically recorded the percentage of fruit that had decayed. Even the most dilute coating that the researchers tested, at 9 percent, slowed decay compared with no coating at all: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
options: after 120 days, about 10% of fruit with the 12% coating had decayed, compared with about 14% of fruit with the 9% coating.
after 90 days, about 9% of fruit with the 9% coating had decayed, compared with about 6% of uncoated fruit.
after 60 days, about 1% of uncoated fruit had decayed, compared with about 2% of fruit with the 9% coating.
after 120 days, about 14% of fruit with the 9% coating had decayed, compared with about 18% of uncoated fruit.

figure.title: Percentage of Ponkan Mandarins Decayed during Storage at 10°C
figure.description: Three lines at 60, 75, 90, 105 and 120 days; y-axis 0 to 20 in steps of 2. Uncoated: about 4.3, 6.7, 9.3, 12.3, 17.7. 9% gum arabic coating: about 1.7, 3.7, 6.0, 9.3, 13.7. 12% gum arabic coating: about 0.7, 1.7, 3.7, 6.0, 9.7. At every time the uncoated line is highest and the 12% line lowest.

items.explanation: The statement needs a comparison between fruit with the 9 percent coating, “the most dilute coating that the researchers tested,” and fruit with “no coating at all.” After 120 days, about 14% of fruit with the 9% coating had decayed, compared with about 18% of uncoated fruit. Choice D completes the statement.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but two coatings compared
A.why_wrong: The values are read correctly, but comparing the 12% and 9% coatings says nothing about whether the 9% coating slowed decay relative to uncoated fruit.

B.why_wrong: At 90 days, about 9% of uncoated fruit and about 6% of fruit with the 9% coating had decayed, the reverse of what this choice states.

C.why_wrong: About 1% decay at 60 days belongs to the 12% coating; uncoated fruit had about 4% decay then, more than the 9% coating’s 2%.

sources.what: Huang, Wan, Zhang, Chen, Chen 2021, Frontiers in Nutrition 8: 717596, Gum Arabic Edible Coating Reduces Postharvest Decay and Alleviates Nutritional Quality Deterioration of Ponkan Fruit During Cold Storage: 9, 12 and 15% GA coatings, storage at 10°C for 120 days, sampled every 15 days; Table 1 decay rate (%) control 4.33, 6.67, 9.33, 12.33, 17.67 at 60-120 days; 9% GA 1.67, 3.67, 6.00, 9.33, 13.67; 12% GA 0.67, 1.67, 3.67, 6.00, 9.67

items.notes: Medium. Food science. The 15% coating is left off the graph. Values from the paper's Table 1 (coated rows begin at day 15; aligned by storage day). Distractors: two coatings compared (A), a swap (B), another line's value (C). Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.

review.notes: values match Table 1 of PMC8558414 (120-day decay 17.67, 13.67, 9.67).

items.subtype: Quotation from a historian supports a claim linking an artist’s work to another role (carving as a form of preaching)
items.passage: Elijah Pierce (1892–1984), the son of a formerly enslaved man, began carving wood as a boy in Mississippi and later spent most of his life working as a barber in Columbus, Ohio. His carvings range from small animal figures to large relief panels crowded with people. A student writing about Pierce argues that much of his carving served the same purpose as preaching: conveying religious and moral lessons through stories.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by a historian would be the most effective evidence for the student to include in support of this claim?
options: “Pierce was licensed as a Baptist preacher in 1920, three years before he settled in Columbus, Ohio, where he would go on to cut hair for most of the rest of his long life.”

“A licensed preacher, Pierce carved his Book of Wood, a set of wooden pages telling the life of Jesus, as a sermon that viewers could read, and he went on to carve many panels that pair a story with a lesson.”
“Pierce began carving at the age of seven with a pocketknife from his father, and his uncle Lewis Wallace later taught him how to carve more complex pieces.”
“Pierce’s work was discovered by the mainstream art world in the early 1970s, and in 1973 he won first prize at an international exhibition of naive art in Zagreb.”
items.explanation: The student argues that Pierce’s carving “served the same purpose as preaching: conveying religious and moral lessons through stories.” Choice B makes that connection: Pierce, himself a licensed preacher, carved the Book of Wood, which tells the life of Jesus, as a sermon viewers could read, and many later panels pair a story with a lesson.

A.recipe: HALF: the preaching without the carving
A.why_wrong: It establishes that Pierce was a preacher and a barber but says nothing about whether his carvings conveyed religious or moral lessons.

C.recipe: OFF: how he learned to carve
C.why_wrong: It explains how Pierce learned his craft, not what his carvings were meant to teach.

D.why_wrong: When and where Pierce’s work won recognition says nothing about whether it served the purpose of preaching.

sources.what: Elijah Pierce (1892-1984), woodcarver; son of a formerly enslaved father; began carving at seven with a pocketknife, taught by his uncle Lewis Wallace; barber from 1908; Baptist preacher's license 1920; settled in Columbus, Ohio, in 1923 as a barber; Book of Wood portrayed the story of Jesus, followed by many similar carvings each with its own story and universal theme; discovered by the mainstream art world in the early 1970s; first prize, International Meeting of Naive Art, Zagreb, 1973; 1982 National Heritage Fellowship

items.notes: Medium. Arts/religion. Replaced Margaret Tafoya before review (Pueblo blackware is too close to CB's Maria Martinez transitions item). Quotations are from an unnamed historian and restate facts from the source page; reading the Book of Wood as a sermon is the historian's interpretation. A is the preaching half without the carving; C and D are off-target biography. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Data completion (one named row, one value)
items.passage: In the 1800s and early 1900s, cities across Latin America built grand opera houses, often hiring European architects and bringing in touring companies of European singers. A student researching these buildings is especially interested in the Teatro Juárez in Guanajuato, Mexico, which President Porfirio Díaz opened with a performance of Giuseppe Verdi’s opera Aida. According to the table, the Teatro Juárez opened in ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

table.title: Opening Years of Five Latin American Opera Houses

items.explanation: The student wants the opening year of “the Teatro Juárez in Guanajuato, Mexico.” In the table, the row for the Teatro Juárez gives 1903, so choice C completes the statement.

A.why_wrong: 1856 is the opening year of the Teatro Solís in Montevideo.

B.why_wrong: 1896 is the opening year of the Teatro Amazonas in Manaus.

D.why_wrong: 1908 is the opening year of the Teatro Colón in Buenos Aires.

sources.what: Teatro Juárez, Guanajuato: inaugurated October 27, 1903, by President Porfirio Díaz with Verdi's Aida

Opening years: Teatro Solís 1856 (Italian architect Carlo Zucchi); Teatro Municipal, Santiago, September 17, 1857 (an Italian company performed Ernani); Teatro Amazonas inaugurated December 31, 1896; Teatro Colón (present building) May 25, 1908

items.notes: Easy. History/arts. Value-only options, each another row's year. Sources: the Wikipedia pages for each theater (Teatro Solís, Municipal Theatre of Santiago, Amazon Theatre, Teatro Colón, Teatro Juárez) checked 2026-10-27. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a hypothesis (one-step operationalization with a comparison group)
items.passage: Psychologist Rachel E. White and colleagues asked four- and six-year-old children to work for 10 minutes on a repetitive computer task, telling them they could take breaks whenever they wished to play an appealing video game. Some children were instructed to think about how they themselves were doing on the task, while others were asked to pretend to be a hardworking character, such as Batman, as they worked. The researchers hypothesized that impersonating such a character would help children persevere.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ hypothesis?
options: Children who pretended to be a hardworking character such as Batman spent more time on the task than children who thought about themselves did.
Six-year-olds spent more time on the task than four-year-olds did, regardless of what they had been asked to think about.
Children who pretended to be Batman reported afterward that they had enjoyed the video game more than the task.
When asked to pretend to be a character, most of the children chose a superhero or other character that they had already seen in movies or on television.
items.explanation: The researchers hypothesized that “impersonating such a character would help children persevere.” If children who pretended to be a hardworking character kept working longer than children who thought about themselves, then impersonating the character helped them persevere, so choice A supports the hypothesis.

B.recipe: SUBJ: the right outcome compared by age, not by instruction
B.why_wrong: A difference between age groups says nothing about whether pretending to be a character helped children persevere.

C.recipe: OFF: enjoyment of the game, not time on task
C.why_wrong: Which activity the children enjoyed more does not show whether impersonating a character kept them working.

D.why_wrong: Where the children had seen their characters says nothing about how long they persevered at the task.

sources.what: White, Prager, Schaefer, Kross, Duckworth, Carlson 2017, Child Development 88(5): 1563-1571, The Batman Effect: 4- and 6-year-olds (N = 180) did a repetitive task for 10 minutes with the option to take breaks to play an attractive video game; children who impersonated an exemplar other such as Batman spent the most time working, then third-person self-talk, then first-person; 6-year-olds persevered longer than 4-year-olds

items.notes: Easy. Psychology. The key states the hypothesis's outcome (time on task) for the right comparison (character vs self). B is a true result of the study about age, not the hypothesis. The study's third condition (third-person self-talk) is left out for length. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Quotation from a participant illustrates a researcher’s two-part claim (soccer and community)
items.passage: The Mathare Youth Sports Association, founded in 1987 in Mathare, a group of informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya, organizes soccer leagues for thousands of young people. Teams earn points not only by winning matches but also by participating in projects to clear garbage from their neighborhoods. Based on interviews with players, a researcher claims that many young people valued the program because it allowed them to improve their community as well as to play soccer.
items.stem: Which quotation from a player would best illustrate the researcher’s claim?
options: “I joined because my older brother played on a team, and our team practiced every afternoon on a field close to my school.”
“The best part was traveling to matches in other parts of Nairobi and getting to meet players from neighborhoods I had never visited before.”
“Some of the clean-up days were hot and tiring, and honestly I only went to them because our team needed the points.”
“I came for the soccer, but I stayed because when we cleared the garbage from our street, people saw young people making Mathare better.”
items.explanation: The researcher claims that young people valued the program “because it allowed them to improve their community as well as to play soccer.” In choice D the player came for soccer but stayed because clearing garbage showed young people “making Mathare better,” which illustrates both parts of the claim.

A.why_wrong: It explains how the player came to the program but says nothing about valuing the chance to improve the community.

B.why_wrong: It values meeting other players, not improving the player’s own community.

C.recipe: LURE: mentions the clean-ups but does not value them
C.why_wrong: The player took part in clean-ups only for the points, so the quotation does not show that improving the community was something the player valued.

sources.what: Mathare Youth Sports Association (MYSA), founded 1987 in Mathare, Nairobi, by Bob Munro; football leagues for thousands of children (14,000 in 1,200 teams in 2010); teams score points for participating in clean-up projects as well as for matches won; UNEP Global 500 award 1999

items.notes: Easy. Sociology. The researcher and the players' quotations are unnamed and invented, as in CB's participant items; the program facts are real. C is the lure: clean-ups mentioned, but valued only for points. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Data completion (the row that is the extreme in two columns at once)
items.passage: Between the 1960s and the 1980s, many British colonies in the Caribbean became independent nations. A student compiling information about five of these countries notices that the country that gained independence most recently is also the smallest of the five in area. That country is ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Grenada.
Saint Kitts and Nevis.
Dominica.
Barbados.

table.title: Independence and Area of Five Caribbean Countries
columns: Year of independence from the United Kingdom

items.explanation: The country must have the latest year of independence and the smallest area. Saint Kitts and Nevis became independent in 1983, later than any other country in the table, and its area of 261 square kilometers is the smallest shown, so choice B completes the statement.

A.why_wrong: Grenada (344 square kilometers) is larger than Saint Kitts and Nevis, and it became independent earlier, in 1974.

C.why_wrong: Dominica, at 750 square kilometers, is the largest of the five countries, and it became independent in 1978.

D.why_wrong: Barbados became independent earliest, in 1966, not most recently.

sources.what: Independence dates and areas (Wikipedia infoboxes): Barbados 30 November 1966, 439 km2; Grenada 7 February 1974, 344 km2; Dominica 3 November 1978, 750 km2; Saint Lucia 22 February 1979, 617 km2; Saint Kitts and Nevis 19 September 1983, 261 km2

items.notes: Easy. History/geography. The extreme in two columns at once (latest year, smallest area), like CB 1.23. Each country's figures from its Wikipedia infobox, checked 2026-10-27. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a single-trait claim (a character reasoning only from what it has seen; poem)
items.passage: “The Tendril’s Fate” is a 1901 poem by Ella Wheeler Wilcox. In the poem, a sprout buried beneath the snow sings about the coming spring while objects around it ridicule its song. Wilcox portrays one of the sprout’s critics as mistaking the limits of its own experience for the limits of the world: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from “The Tendril’s Fate” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “‘How foolish your songs!’ said a lump of clay; / ‘What is there, I ask, to prove them? / Just look at the walls between you and the day, / Now, have you the strength to move them?’”
“Under the snow, in the dark and the cold, / A pale little sprout was humming; / Sweetly it sang, ’neath the frozen mould, / Of the beautiful days that were coming.”
“A pebble spoke next: ‘You are quite absurd,’ / It said, ‘with your song’s insistence; / For I never saw a tree or a bird, / So of course there are none in existence.’”
“‘But I know, I know,’ the tendril cried, / In beautiful sweet unreason; / Till lo! from its prison, glorified, / It burst in the glad spring season.”
items.explanation: The claim is that one critic mistakes the limits of its own experience for the limits of the world. In choice C the pebble reasons, “I never saw a tree or a bird, / So of course there are none in existence”: because it has not seen such things, it concludes they do not exist.

A.recipe: OFF: a critic who doubts for a different reason
A.why_wrong: The clay mocks the sprout by pointing to the walls around it and its lack of strength, an argument about obstacles, not one based on what the clay has never seen.

B.recipe: SUBJ: the sprout, not a critic
B.why_wrong: These lines describe the sprout singing hopefully, not any critic’s reasoning.

D.recipe: SUBJ: the sprout’s confidence and the outcome
D.why_wrong: These lines show the sprout’s certainty and its emergence in spring; they do not show a critic judging the world by its own experience.

sources.what: Ella Wheeler Wilcox, The Tendril's Fate, in Poems of Power (Chicago: W. B. Conkey, copyright 1901; Gutenberg text from the London Gay and Hancock edition); all four stanzas checked as exact text, with inner double quotes rendered as single quotes and the italic I set roman

items.notes: Easy. Poem. Single-trait claim about the pebble; the clay is the other critic with a different argument. The collection's copyright pages (archive.org scan, poemsofpower00wilc) show 1901, 1902 and 1903; the poem is in the earliest edition scanned. Blind solve by the writer on the rendered item, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

review.notes: all four stanzas exact against Gutenberg 6667 (inner double quotes as single, italic I set roman).
